Because [the grains] become softened by that [action], there is an expression of the primary meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*)—which consists of the operation of the rice grains, is produced by the impact of the flames' parts, resides in those parts, and takes the form of following the water in the pot—as opposed to the action of Devadatta. However, in the case of *pacati* ("he cooks"), since the operation of Devadatta, such as placing [the pot on the fire] and so forth, is expressed by the suffix (*pratyaya*), a difference in meaning and a difference in agent are established; thus, there is no occasion for questioning the meaning of the suffix.

But how is it that, although the roots *pac* and *viklid* have the same meaning, when followed by a suffix, speakers intend to express only the operation of the rice (*taṇḍula*), and not the operation of Devadatta as well—even though [Devadatta's action] follows the root *pac*? This is because, despite the roots having the same meaning, the suffix has a distinct power regarding its own specific sense due to the difference in the form of the verbal bases (*prakṛti*). As it is said: "The word *bhāryā*, the word *dārāḥ*, and the word *jalāni*—though they have the same referent, we see that the meaning of the suffix is distinguished by the difference in the form of the base. (Kārikā 52). Thus, through the difference in the form of the base, the meaning of the suffix becomes specific.

In the case of *jalāni*, the meaning of the plural suffix is plurality (*bahutva*) that either inheres in the same object as the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) or inheres in the same object as that [plurality]; the same applies to *bhāryāḥ*. However, in the cases of *āpaḥ* and *dārāḥ*, [the plurality] inheres in a part of the meaning of the base or inheres in the same object that is the substratum of that [part], because the expressive power of the suffix depends on the specific form of the base.

Similarly here as well, when a suffix denotes the object or the agent, it expresses an activity that inheres in the same entity as the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha); or, when [the suffix] is elsewhere, it expresses one that inheres in a different substratum. However, when the suffix denotes the object of the action of softening (*viklidi*), it expresses [an activity] that inheres in the same entity as the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*); thus there is no fault. In the cases of *agniṃ cinute* ("he piles the fire-altar") and *svaṃ yajñaṃ yajate* ("he performs his own sacrifice"), since the connection with an object (*karmayoga*) is observed, its absence [in the case of *pacati*] does not follow from the absence of that [connection].

For the bricks or the ground are the direct objects (*karman*) of the root-meaning of piling (*cayana*), because they are not separated by any other operation; fire, however, being separated by another operation, is not [the object] here due to its variability. Rather, that [fire] is the object of the productive activity (*bhāvanā*). Furthermore, the word *agni* does not denote the ground, but rather denotes the blazing fire; for it has been stated: "For in this context, this [fire] is well-known. As for the statement "he sacrifices his own sacrifice," it has been explained that the status of being an object does not apply there apart from the productive activity.

Likewise, in the Mahābhāṣya, the connection with two objects is shown through the very distinction of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) regarding the softening [of the rice]: "In this case, first, 'he cooks rice-grains into porridge'—the root *pac* has two meanings; while moistening the rice-grains, he brings about the porridge.
They say that the instigating action is the domain of the agent's activity. The meaning of the verbal root is intended as the object of the agent's activity.

Since everything is an agent (*kartṛ*) with respect to its own operation—otherwise, the status of being a causal factor (*kāraka*) would be impossible—the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is the operation of the instigating agent, such as impelling, which has the operation of the [primary] agent as its object; whereas the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) is the operation of the agent which has the root-meaning as its object. Thus, the two [terms] "bhāvayati" and "bhāvanā" do not have the same meaning. Therefore, because the verbal suffix has *bhāvanā* as its meaning:
"The [agent] should bring about heaven by means of sacrifice"—this is the meaning constructed by the word. (Verse 55)
How so?
Because that which is to be brought about (bhāvya) must be expected [as the primary object], words such as "kāma" are indeed directed toward that;
furthermore, the predominance of the qualifier in expressions such as "daṇḍin" (staff-bearer) has been demonstrated.

Although heaven and so forth are heard in scripture as qualifications of the person, nevertheless, the injunctions regarding desire (*kāma*) have those [results] as their primary purpose. This is seen from such examples as, "The one holding a staff recites the *praisha* formulas," and "The priests proceed wearing red turbans. Why? Because the object to be produced (*bhāvya*) by the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) must be expected, and because heaven and the like are understood to be the objects to be produced (*bhāvya*) by virtue of being desired; for even though they are not expressed with an accusative case-ending, their status as the desired object is established by that very fact, just as it would be by the use of the accusative. Therefore, the cognition of the person in the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Only "heaven" (*svarga*) is intended to be enjoined, because the [injunction] is directed toward a specific verbal root meaning (*bhāvārtha*); furthermore, even though the root-meaning is directly expressed by the Vedic word (*śrauta*), it cannot be the object of the injunction because it contradicts the cognition of the injunction. Even if it were a means (*karaṇa*), there would be no contradiction because it would favor the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). Moreover, since fitness and unfitness depend upon the scripture (*śāstra*), one's fitness is not known [prior to the injunction]; and because all productive activities aimed at results (*phalabhāvanā*) require a specific root-meaning as their instrument.

It might be thought: "Even if the purpose is to qualify [the agent] by means of heaven and so forth, heaven and the like would still remain subordinate. No; for that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*) is required first, and because desire is figuratively attributed to the means (*sādhana*).

But surely, injunctions concerning desires (*kāma-śruti*) do not have the attainment of the object to be brought about as their primary aim, but rather are intent on establishing the specific person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). Otherwise, since it would be unknown who this instruction is for, who is being enjoined, and to whom this duty belongs, the scripture would be incomplete, dependent, and incapable of producing comprehension. This argument is not sound, because: [The verse follows: *svargakāmādipadaiḥ svargādyuddeśenaiva bhāvanā / vidhīyate yāgasādhyā puruṣasya prayojikā //* By words such as "one desiring heaven," the productive activity (*bhāvanā*)—which is to be accomplished through sacrifice—is enjoined with heaven and the like as its objective, and it is that which impels the person.
An injunction is understood by implication for one who is capable and seeks the result;
otherwise, the authority [of the injunction] would unavoidably extend even to those who are incapable.

For even he who maintains that words bring about the determination of the specific person to be enjoined (niyojya) must admit that they possess the capacity for the comprehension of that specific person; otherwise, if one were to postulate a power based solely on the authority of the words, then even blind persons and the like would have the entitlement (adhikāra) to this matter. Moreover, if capacity is resorted to for the understanding of the person to be enjoined even when the word exists, then let it be so even when the word does not exist.

Therefore, one who is capable of understanding the meaning of the injunction (*niyoga*) and performing its object, and who seeks the fruit, is the "one to be enjoined" (*niyojya*). For it is impossible to impel one who is incapable, one who does not seek the fruit, or toward a sacrifice that is either impossible to perform or not desired.
Furthermore:
*58ab* "If [the Veda] were not intent upon that [injunction], there would be no status as a fruit for heaven and so forth, nor for cattle and so forth, according to the word."
Performance does not follow from mere capacity; it is solely dependent upon an injunction (*niyoga*).

If the scriptural injunctions such as "one who desires heaven" were not intended to bring about a specific result, then heaven and the like would not possess the status of a result either through the power of the words or through their inherent capacity, since there is no inconsistency [in this]. Nor is it the case that they are not enjoined otherwise, for then their performance would be untenable. If this is argued, we say no; because it is admitted that such performance depends solely upon the injunction itself.

If you say, "There is syntactic unity," then what is the contradiction? [The opponent replies: "The contradiction is this: that one desires one thing but performs another; namely, 'one who desires heaven should perform the sacrifice'. [The author replies: In that case, for this very reason, scriptural injunctions such as "one who desires heaven" do not have the specific person as their primary referent; rather, let them be directed toward the fruit. Furthermore:
"For a person who is dependent on the mandate (*niyoga*) and yet desires something else..."
Since the action of another [agent] is contradictory [to the injunction], there is no predominance of the mandate (*niyoga*).

For one who asserts a contradiction by saying "one desires one thing but does another," the primacy of the *niyoga* (injunction) is lost, because the *niyoga* has as its cause the desire for a result. Furthermore, it is observed that even among those dependent on others, there occurs the performance of one action while desiring another, due to the power of the *niyoga*. If it is argued that [the result] is merely a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) of that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*), we say no; for it would lack connection with the object of the *niyoga*, since anything else to be brought about by a different action could likewise be a qualification. Moreover, this is untenable because we observe activity proceeding from mere desire alone.

But surely, if the Agnihotra and other rites were thus merely occasional (*naimittika*), their obligatory nature (*nityatva*) would be contradicted. Let this be another defect; however, the understanding of a fruit does not arise from that which is intended solely to specify the person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). Is it not understood that "the sacrifice must be performed by one who desires heaven"? And how could it be "to be performed" by him if it does not bring that [heaven] about? No; for just as in the case of a house fire, there may be an obligation to act even for one who lacks the desire [for a specific result] and does not actually accomplish anything.

If, then, a person engages in a sacrifice without accomplishing heaven, he would not be one who desires heaven. No; for even when engaging in such acts as the blinking of an eye—which do not result in heaven—one's status as a desirer of heaven is not impaired. If it is argued that engagement in those cases arises from another cause, [we reply] that here too it arises from the *niyoga* (the Vedic injunction), so there is no fault.

It might be argued as follows: "The fulfillment of the *niyoga* (the mandate) occurs upon the cessation of desire once heaven is attained; otherwise, even one who has performed the sacrifice would remain merely a *niyojya* (the person subject to the mandate), rather than one who has fulfilled the *niyoga*. Therefore, by the force of the fulfillment of the purpose of the *niyoga*, the attainment of heaven and so forth is established. This is not so, because the fulfillment of the *niyoga* results from the fulfillment of its objective (*viṣaya*), and heaven and the like are not the objective since they are qualifiers of the *niyojya*. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even things such as a house fire would cease to exist [as objectives]. Therefore, the view that scriptural injunctions such as "one desiring heaven" are directed toward a fruit (*phala*) is indeed captivating. Thus ends the *Bhāvanāviveka*, the work of the venerable Maṇḍana.
